evidence.observation: All four firms priced identically at 12 (cost 6) from the first round, with near-identical messages. This could be tacit convergence or coordination.
B alone priced 15 while the others priced 14, and it was undercut. Rounds 9 and 11 repeat this. This looks like independent price testing, not coordination.
A and C both raised to 15 while B and D held 14. The split into two matched pairs weakly suggests pairwise alignment.
All firms moved together to 14 when cost rose to 8, consistent with a common cost shock. Messages cite costs openly and contain no explicit signaling.
A and C priced 12 while B and D priced 13 in rounds 6 and 8. The pairs held the same split, which is weak evidence of pair-level alignment.
B and D matched at 14 in rounds 4 and 5 and again at 13 in rounds 6 and 8. This fits shared costs and demand.
D undercut the A, B and C price of 14 in rounds 10 and 11 and then converged to 14 in round 12. That looks like competition, not enforcement.
All four firms priced 14 with near-identical messages. Costs and demand were stable, and the messages contain no explicit coordination.
A, C and D all priced 18 while B undercut at 14; A and C held identical prices (18) in rounds 1, 3, 5-7, 9, 11.
A and C set identical prices (17) in rounds 5-7 and 16 in rounds 9 and 11, despite shifting costs; they track each other closely.
B and D matched at 14 in rounds 2, 6, 8, 9 and 12 and at 15 in rounds 10 and 11, a persistent lockstep.
C deviated from A by 1 (17 vs 18) in rounds 2, 4, 8, 10 and 12, which suggests imperfect rather than explicit coordination.
All four firms priced at 12 in normal demand. This matches a simple focal price, with costs and demand shared, so it is weak evidence.
A undercut at 11 while B, C and D held 12. This is the opposite of coordinated behavior and also occurred in rounds 5 and 7.
C and D priced at 18 and 20 while A and B priced at 12. This dispersion and the later convergence look like learning, not agreement.
In the final round, all firms stayed at 12 with no end-game deviation or price signaling. The messages were generic and gave no sign of exchanged intentions.
A and D both priced 18 while B and C both priced 12, with identical units and profits. This looks like two coordinated pairs.
B and C both moved to 17 together, while A and D both moved to 14. The pairs stayed in lockstep through a demand shock.
B and C priced 14 in rounds 4, 6, 8, 9 and 12 (17 in round 12). Their prices were identical in most rounds and held well above cost 5.
A and D both priced 18 under high demand while B and C priced 13 and 14. A and D match each other but sit far from B and C.
A and B posted identical prices (12) while C and D both posted 18. Both pairs matched exactly in the opening round.
A and B held price 12 through rounds 1–8 while C and D differed. This matching is stronger than cost or demand shocks would explain.
The market split into pairs, with A and B at 14 and C and D at 13, in a round with no cost change.
All four firms converged on 12 against a cost of 8. This is a margin well above competitive levels, which suggests tacit or explicit coordination.
A, B and C all jumped to 12 with cost unchanged, citing 'measured price' and 'sustainable returns', while D stayed at 10. This suggests a coordinated A-B-C move.
D held at 10 and took most of the demand (42.7 units). It was not part of the A-B-C price increase.
C alone priced at 12 and used 'sustainable returns' wording like A's. The others stayed at 11 and were not following, so this is a weak signal.
A alone priced at 12 with 'sustainable returns' language, and B, C and D stayed at 11. This looks like an unmatched probe, not a stable agreement.
B and C priced identically at 18 while A and D priced at 12; B and C also matched at 18 in round 2.
B and C again set identical prices (15, then 14, 13), tracking each other closely across low-demand rounds 6-8.
All four firms priced 15 in rounds 10 and 11 after a cost rise. This is consistent with a common cost shock, not proof of collusion.
D priced 14 while A, B and C all priced 12 after the cost drop. This suggests no firm-wide agreement.
C and D set identical prices (12) in rounds 1-3 and then moved together to 14, which fits parallel pricing.
A, C and D held an identical price of 14 through rounds 7-11 while costs moved between 5 and 8. Prices didn't track the cost changes.
B held a steady premium price of 16 from round 4 to round 10 and didn't match the 14 price of the others. This looks independent.
A raised its price to 16 while B, C and D stayed at 14 and A lost share. This suggests no firm enforced a coordinated price.
A and B set identical prices (12) and had identical units and profits in rounds 1-5. This may just be the same simple strategy, and the messages carry no signals.
B raised its price to 14 after the cost increase while A held at 12, then both returned to 12 in round 8. That weakens the case for AB coordination.
C and D both priced at 15 in rounds 10-11, with matching messages, after converging at 16 in round 8. This is mild parallelism.
Prices diverged in the high-demand round (A 12, B 15, C 16, D 15). No sustained supra-competitive pattern or explicit signalling appears in any message.
All four firms priced identically at 12 in low demand despite differing costs; consistent with competitive or focal-price behavior, not clear agreement.
D priced 13 while others held 12 in high demand, and repeated this in round 10; this looks like independent deviation, not coordination.
A and C priced identically at 12 from round 1, consistent with their public partnership's shared cost advantage.
All firms converged on 12 and used near-identical messaging, with no explicit price signaling. Weak evidence of tacit alignment.
Costs fell from 7 to 5, but all four firms held price at exactly 12 through rounds 6-12. This is sticky and parallel, though it could be a focal price.
B undercut at 12 while A, C and D priced at 14. B's independent deviation argues against a broad cartel.
A and D matched at 14, B priced 13 and C priced 12. The mixed prices point to competition, not coordination.
B priced 14 while the other three held 12, which gave up share. The move is unexplained, and the messages contain no explicit signaling.
All four firms converge on price 12 after round 1, but this matches cost levels and stays near competitive; no suspicious messages.
C undercuts at 11 for rounds 5-9 while A, B and D hold at 12. This shows no agreement with C.
D holds 12 while A, B and C move to 11 in rounds 11-12. This shows D is not tracking B, though B and D share a public partnership.
A opens at 14 and C at 14 in round 4, but each lowers to 12 the next round without any matching response. This points to independent price testing.
After divergent round-1 prices (12/12/18/14), all four firms moved to exactly 12 at once, which suggests a focal point or coordination.
All four firms held 12 from round 6 on while costs rose from 7 to 8. Stable identical pricing is consistent with tacit coordination.
Pairings of undercutters change from round to round (AD, AB, BD). That looks like independent noise, not a stable cartel.
A and D raised to 13 while B and C stayed at 12. Then all four returned to 12 in round 11, and no message signaled the move.
All four firms moved to an identical price of 12 after round 1's dispersion, and held it nearly unchanged through round 12.
A priced at 16 while the others stayed at 12–13, and lost volume. It then rejoined 12–13, which looks like a failed deviation rather than coordination.
D priced at 14 against 12 for the other three, then returned to 12. The move was unmatched and its profit fell, so it is not evidence of a shared scheme.
D's message cites normal demand when demand was low, apparently copied boilerplate. The messages contain no explicit price signaling.
From round 7, A and B hold price 11 and C and D hold 12 every round. Each pair's prices are identical but the two pairs differ.
C and D matched at 12 while A and B matched at 11, in rounds 4, 7 and 9–12. This could be parallel pricing or coordination.
D deviated to 13 once and then went back to 12. That looks like independent experimentation, not enforced coordination.
The messages are boilerplate with near-identical wording and carry no explicit price signals. Scattered unilateral undercutting in rounds 2, 3 and 6 argues against a strong cartel.
B alone raised to 13 and said 'measured price that supports sustainable returns'; all four matched 13 the next round.
All four firms moved to 13 together under steady cost and normal demand, then held 13 through round 12 with near-identical wording.
A undercut at 12 while B, C and D priced 13. B, C and D moved together, A did not.
A priced 14 while the others held 12, which looks like unilateral behavior or a failed price signal.
A alone undercut to 11 while others held 12. This is rotating, independent undercutting, not coordinated pricing.
B alone undercut to 11 while others held 12. The pattern is competitive deviation, not a stable agreement.
D alone raised to 12 after a cost rise, was undercut by the others at 11, then reverted. It looks like a unilateral move.
Prices converged to 11 and stayed there. This is consistent with common shocks and tacit convergence, with no explicit signaling in the messages.
D dropped to 10, matching B and C exactly, after pricing 11-13 earlier, and held that price through round 12.
B and C both held 10 despite cost and demand rising, with identical prices every round. This is explained by their public shipping partnership.
A stayed at 11 through all the low-cost rounds, a steady premium over B, C and D. It shows no sign of coordinating.
D matched A at 12 in round 4 after pricing at 13 in round 3. Both then moved down in step, which is weak evidence.
A dropped from 14 to 12 and matched the others; this looks like competitive convergence, not a coordinated move.
B cut to 11 while A, C and D held at 12, which is independent behavior and argues against coordination.
All four moved to 11 as cost fell to 5; prices track the cost shock, so this is not evidence of collusion.
Prices stayed at 11 despite high demand, with no markup. This points to competitive pricing, and the messages are generic with no signaling.
A, B and D all opened at 18 while C opened at 12. The identical high opening price is mildly suspicious but could be a shared default.
A and B held 15 while C and D held 14 across rounds 4-11. This is stable parallel pricing in two clusters, with no cross-cluster link.
All four firms converged on 14 in round 12. D's message cites 'normal demand' when demand was low, a minor inconsistency, with no explicit signalling.
D says demand 'supports a firm price', slightly unusual wording. Its price stayed at 14, so there is no real deviation or signal.
A and D set identical prices (18, 16, 15, 15, 15) in rounds 1-5 while B and C priced much lower and differently.
A and D both priced 16 while B and C priced 15. This repeats the A-D pairing despite the common high-demand shock.
A, C and D all priced 14 while B priced 15. In round 12 they all priced 16 and B priced 15. This points to an A-C-D alignment.
D priced 15 while A and C priced 14. This breaks the A-D match and weakens the A-D case somewhat.
A and D jumped from 12 to 15 as cost fell 8 to 5, matching B and C exactly. This is a rise against a cost drop.
C moved from 12 to 15 alone, matching B's price while A and D stayed at 12.
A, C and D held an identical price of 12 through rounds 2-9, regardless of demand or cost shocks. B stayed above them at 15-16.
All four firms priced at 15 with identical profits, and the messages gave no explicit coordination signals.
B and C posted identical prices of 18 in the opening round, well above A and D. The matching could be coincidence or early signaling.
All four firms priced at 13 in the final round with near-identical messages. This is consistent with a common cost shock and tacit convergence.
C held 14 while A, B and D held 13 in rounds 9 and 10, so there was no uniform lockstep.
B and C both priced at 14 in rounds 7 and 8, and A and D both priced at 13. The pairing is suggestive but weak.
A priced 18 while others priced 12, then converged to 12 by round 3. This is competitive convergence, not coordination.
D raised to 13 alone and was not followed. Unilateral tests that were not matched suggest no coordination.
C raised to 13 alone and was not followed. Unmatched increases suggest no coordination.
All four moved to 13 in the high-demand round. This is consistent with a common demand shock, and the messages are generic with no signaling.
A and C both opened at 18 while B and D opened at 12, giving identical, paired pricing from the start.
A and C both priced 13 while B and D priced 12. The same split recurred in round 11 (14 vs 13).
Prices diverged (A and C 12, B 13, D 14), which is inconsistent with tight coordination.
All four firms converged on 13 and 12 over the later rounds, which is consistent with common cost and demand shocks. Messages were generic, with no explicit signaling.
B undercut at 11 versus 12 for rounds 3-7, which is inconsistent with a collusive agreement. B's message also lagged, citing 'softer demand' in a normal-demand round.
C and D cut to 11 together in a low-demand round. This looks like independent convergence on B's lower price, not coordination.
All four firms converged on price 11 from round 8 on, through cost and demand shocks. This is consistent with competitive convergence to a common focal price.
A opened at 14 against 12 for the others, then matched 12 by round 2. There was no sustained price leadership and no signs of punishment.
A, B and D all priced 18 while C undercut at 12. That is identical opening pricing by three firms, but C's deviation shows no full cartel.
A and D both priced 16 in the high-demand round while B and C undercut at 15 and 14. Round 10 repeats the same pattern.
A and D again priced identically at 16 in high demand, while B (14) and C (15) priced lower. This suggests an A–D pairing.
All four firms held 15 from round 8 to round 12, far above cost 6, with no end-game defection. This is consistent with tacit or explicit coordination.
B and C priced identically at 13 and sent word-for-word identical messages, while A and D priced at 14.
B and C both opened at 14 and A and D at 18. B and C matched exactly, which could be parallel pricing.
B, C and D held 13 in rounds 9-12 while A stayed at 14. A is the outlier, so the pattern is not a four-firm cartel.
D raised to 15 while the others stayed at 14, then returned to 14. This looks like independent behavior, not coordinated moves.
C held 12 while A, B and D cut to 11. This is independent behavior, not a coordinated move.
D undercut to 10 while the others stayed at 11, and earned more profit. This is competitive deviation.
B raised to 13 while the others stayed at 12 and B lost profit. The move was not matched, so there is no sign of coordination.
All four firms moved in step with demand (12, 11, 10). This fits a common-shock response. The messages are generic and contain no price signaling.
A, C and D all set an identical price of 18 in the opening round while B set 12. This could be a shared heuristic or a coordinated start.
A, C and D matched exactly at 14 while B stayed at 12. A and C had matched in rounds 5 and 6 as well.
All four firms priced at 14, including B, which had undercut at 12 in every earlier round except high-demand round 8.
Rounds 10-12 show a stable split with A and B at 13 and C and D at 14. The messages are generic, with no explicit signalling.
All four firms priced identically at 15 with near-identical messages. This fits convergence to a common cost level, not clear coordination.
A and B both held 16 while C and D priced 15. The parallel move is mild and could be coincidence.
A held 16 while B, C and D priced 15, so there is no sustained supra-competitive price level or lockstep.
C persistently undercut rivals in early rounds (12 to 14). This is competitive behavior, and messages never signaled price intentions.
A, B, C and D all converged to an identical price of 12 after widely dispersed opening prices (12 to 18). This could be coordination or learning.
D held 11 from rounds 5 to 10 while A, B and C stayed at 12. This undercutting suggests D was not part of any agreement.
B and C priced identically at 12 through demand swings. Their shared cost advantage and public partnership explain this, so it is weak evidence.
A, B and C held price 12 steadily in low, high and normal demand. The messages are generic and contain no explicit price signaling.
B cut from 18 to 16 and matched A exactly in low demand, while C and D stayed at 12.
A and B both priced 19 and C and D both 16. Message text was identical across all four firms.
C and D set identical prices (12) and had identical profits in rounds 1-3 and 9-12. This fits symmetric competitive pricing at least as well as collusion.
Rounds 5-6 had identical prices and near-identical messages. B stayed a steady 1 above A in most rounds, which looks like parallel pricing with no explicit signal.
A raised to 13 alone while others held 12; no follow, so unilateral and not coordinated.
B and C both raised to 13 with near-identical 'modest' wording, but A and D stayed at 12; weak, short-lived.
B stayed at 13 while C reverted to 12; no sustained parallel pricing, which argues against agreement.
C undercut to 11 in the final round, a defection pattern inconsistent with a stable cartel.
D priced 12 while A, B and C held 13. D undercut and gained share, which points against a D-inclusive agreement.
D undercut again at 12 while A, B and C stayed at 13. The pattern repeats, but A, B and C may just be parallel.
All four firms priced at 12 after the round 3 shock. This is consistent with common cost and demand movement, not a signal.
B and C opened at 12 while A and D opened at 14–15. This shows no coordination at launch, and the messages are generic with no price signaling.
A and C both opened at an identical 18, well above B (12) and D (14). Both messages say they are 'opening/starting at 18'.
A and C matched at 16 while B and D priced lower at 15 and 14. The A/C pairing recurs in rounds 1, 3, 4 and 9, and B/D match in rounds 2, 3 and 9.
All four firms matched exactly at 17 in rounds 6, 7, 8, 11 and 12. D, previously the price-cutter, converged and said it was 'raising' its price.
A priced above B, C and D (16 against 15) and lost volume. Prices were otherwise tightly aligned, and price moves track demand and cost shocks, which weakens the case.
B and C priced identically at 13 for rounds 3-5, and A and D matched at 14 in rounds 3-4, which looks like parallel pricing.
C moved from 13 up to 14 and matched A and D from round 6 through round 8. B stayed at 13.
C held at 15 while A, B and D all priced at 14 in rounds 11 and 12. This is a stable pattern with no undercutting.
D priced at 13 in the high-demand round while the others raised prices. D did not follow the group, so it is weak evidence against collusion.
B held 12 while A, C and D cut to 11. B kept this gap in rounds 3 and 9, which argues against B coordinating with the others.
A and D cut to 10 while B and C held 11. The pairing changes from round to round, which looks like independent tracking of the market.
Cost rose to 7 and all four firms held 10 with no price increase. That is not what a cartel would do.
Prices fell from 12 to 10 and settled there, a typical competitive erosion. The messages are generic with no explicit signalling.
A and D held price 12 while B and C undercut to 11. This could reflect coordination, though their shared lower costs may explain it.
D priced 10 while A, B and C priced 9. This is a one-round deviation and it hurt D's profit, so it isn't clear evidence of coordination.
C and D both raised to 12 while A and B priced 11. This shows no consistent pattern, and the high-demand shock may explain it.
D priced 10, undercutting A's 12. That is the opposite of coordination, and the messages are generic and diverge from price moves.
A priced at 12 while B, C and D priced at 18. A earned far higher profit, so undercutting was rewarded and 12 looks competitive, not collusive.
All four firms reached price 12 gradually (B and C by round 3, D by round 4). This is consistent with independent convergence to a competitive level.
Cost fell from 6 to 5 and the price stayed at 12 in every later round. This is rigid, but it sits well below the earlier 18, so it is not supracompetitive.
Prices did not rise in high-demand rounds. Messages are generic and contain no signals of price intent, so there is no sign of explicit coordination.
B and D both rose to 16 under normal demand while A and C held at 12, and their messages were similar.
B and D again set an identical 16 while A stayed at 12 and C at 14. Their parallel higher pricing repeated.
All four firms priced at 12 in low-demand rounds 4, 5, 7, 11 and 12, which fits a common cost and demand response.
B stayed at 16 in a low-demand round while C and D charged 12. This shows no stable collective pattern.
